title: One batch at a time, stopping before the line (Stage B slice 3)
body:
Slice 3 of `docs/plans/oracle/stage-b-extraction.md` — **OD-22**, **BL-23** items 5–6, **R7**, **R26**, **R27**. R7's promised continue command, which nothing has ever provided.

Written blind on both halves: the implementation and the two test files were authored by agents that never saw each other's work.

### What it does

**`spend.py` is the R26 guard.** `Weekly (7-day)` governs, per the owner's ruling of 2026-08-25, matched by that exact label and never `limits[0]`. The ceiling is `baseline + 0.10`, clamped at 1.0 — **R26 caps the extraction EFFORT, not the account**, so a run starting at 43% stops at 53% rather than refusing outright.

A percent outside 0.0–1.0 is **refused rather than rescaled**: guessing the scale either disables the guard or makes it refuse everything, silently either way.

`Reading.source` records which reader answered. The `claude -p "/usage"` fallback **starts a session and so spends against the very limit it reads**, so a reading that perturbed the meter is different evidence from one that did not.

**`commands/extract.py`** takes three readings — before, at the halfway bundle, and after. The part-way one is what makes it a guard rather than a receipt. One retry on a claims file that fails validation, then set aside, named, and **the batch continues**: halting would strand the bundles already paid for. A stop is not a rollback — everything extracted stays extracted, everything ingested stays ingested (R27), and the exit code is non-zero so nothing mistakes a partial batch for a whole one.

### Blind test authorship

`Blind-Tests: stage-b-extraction-3`. **73 cases** across the two files the plan names, proved under **17 deliberate mutations** — an absolute 10% ceiling, an unclamped ceiling, `limits[0]`, a 0–100 percent scale, the fallback reader tried first, an unrecorded source, only two readings, the ceiling checked after the batch, rollback on stop, deleted model output, exit 0 on a stop, remaining bundles omitted from the output, halt instead of set aside, no retry, a silent set-aside, a wrong batch tag, and `--batch` ignored.

Two design choices in those tests worth keeping. The ceiling is exercised from a **0.43 baseline throughout**, so an absolute-10% guard refuses the run instead of quietly passing — a suite starting at 0.02 would never have noticed. And both files carry an autouse fixture that **fails any test starting a real process**, so a seam guessed wrong cannot silently become a real `claude -p "/usage"` that spends against the limit under test.

**It assembled with zero behavioural disagreements** — 1807 passing on the first run. Both agents had flagged the seam as unspecified and reached different patch points; it worked because `take_reading` calls subprocess internally, which is what the tests faked.

### The plan contradicts itself, and both agents found it independently

Slice 1's `claimstore.append_claims` **refuses a batch it already holds** — the mirror of R27, no completed work silently rewritten. Slice 3's text says "extract one bundle, **ingest it**, read again". Appending per bundle would be refused from the second bundle onward. **Both cannot be taken literally.**

Both agents resolved it the same way without conferring: validate per bundle, append once per run. The test author asserted the OUTCOME — what `read_claims` holds when the run ends — and never the timing of appends, precisely so an implementation batching its appends would pass and one appending per bundle would crash visibly at assembly.

The consequence is now in `docs/architecture.md`: a stopped batch's remaining bundles cannot later join the store under the same batch number without moving the store aside. **Nothing model-produced is lost** — slice 2 writes every claims file as it is produced — so the remedy is a deliberate act rather than a re-spend.

### One addition beyond the Signatures block

`UsageUnreadable`, raised when neither reader answers. The plan does not say what happens then, and inventing a reading would let the batch run unwatched while printing a number from nowhere.

### Seven type errors, fixed by the test author rather than by me

`mypy src tests` failed on the blind file: three `arg-type` from the fake's `Sequence[object]` argv, four `func-returns-value` from `assert check(...) is None` (`check` is declared `-> None`, so mypy refuses to let its result be used at all).

I asked its author to fix them **in its own worktree** and amend, so `blind-tests.sh` has nothing to report and the file stays theirs rather than carrying an edit of mine. It moved the assertion into one helper with a single scoped `type: ignore`, kept every call site's message, rebuilt its reference implementation to verify rather than reasoning about mypy in the abstract, and **re-ran the mutations that exercise those exact assertions** to prove nothing was weakened. `blind-tests.sh` reports both files unmodified since their authoring commit.

### Two things this slice does not do

- **`./scripts/run.sh extract --batch N`** — the plan's Delivers line — does not work. `run.sh` validates a fixed stage list, forwards no flags, and its own header promises that nothing in it spends money. It is in no slice's Files list and is left alone. Extraction runs as `uv run find-best-mobo extract --batch 1`. Recorded as a rough edge; the plan's Delivers line is what is wrong.
- **`cli.py`** is in the Files list and is not touched: dispatch is dynamic.

### Verified locally

1807 passing (73 new). `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .` clean. `mypy src tests` clean over 57 files. `plan-resolve.sh` resolves this plan. `blind-tests.sh` green.
